items.followUp: Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Names the two main types of cellular organization.
rubric.description: Cellular organization is of two main types: prokaryotic and eukaryotic.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both types.

rubric.why: Describes the defining feature and location of DNA in prokaryotic cells.
rubric.description: Prokaryotic cells lack a true nucleus; their DNA lies in a nucleoid region.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both that there is no true nucleus and that DNA lies in a nucleoid.

rubric.why: Gives an example of a prokaryotic organism.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example, such as bacteria.

rubric.why: States key features of eukaryotic cells.
rubric.description: Eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating both features.

rubric.why: Gives an example of organisms with eukaryotic cells.
rubric.description: Plants, animals and fungi are made of eukaryotic cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a correct example such as plants, animals or fungi.

modelAnswer: Cells show two main types of cellular organization: prokaryotic and eukaryotic.
Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound, true nucleus; their DNA lies in a nucleoid region in the cytoplasm.
Bacteria are examples of prokaryotic organisms.
Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound, true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Plants, animals and fungi are made of eukaryotic cells.

items.followUp: Explain the rules of binomial nomenclature and give two scientific names.

rubric.why: Explains why common names are not reliable worldwide.
rubric.description: Common names vary between languages or regions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that common names vary between languages or regions.

rubric.why: Describes the confusion caused by variable common names.
rubric.description: The same organism may have different common names, or one common name may refer to different organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing either form of naming confusion.

rubric.why: States the advantage of using scientific names.
rubric.description: Scientific names provide standardized names used internationally.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that scientific names are standardized or universal.

rubric.why: Gives the two parts of a binomial scientific name.
rubric.description: A scientific name consists of the genus name followed by the species name.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying both parts in the correct order.

rubric.why: Illustrates scientific naming with a correct example.
rubric.description: Homo sapiens is the scientific name of humans; Mangifera indica is the scientific name of mango.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for at least one correct scientific name.

modelAnswer: Common names vary from one language or region to another, so they may cause confusion.
The same organism may have different common names, and one common name may sometimes be used for different organisms.
Scientists therefore use scientific names, which are standardized internationally.
In binomial nomenclature, each scientific name has two words: the genus name followed by the species name.
For example, the scientific name of humans is Homo sapiens, and that of mango is Mangifera indica.

items.followUp: Describe the structure of a chloroplast and state the functions of its main parts.

rubric.why: Describes the outer structure of plastids.
rubric.description: A plastid is enclosed by a double membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that plastids have a double membrane.

rubric.why: Describes the internal structure of a chloroplast.
rubric.description: The stroma is the fluid matrix; thylakoids are arranged in stacks called grana.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the stroma, thylakoids and grana.
Award 1 mark for linking chloroplasts with photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Names a plastid type and its characteristic contents or role.
rubric.description: Chromoplasts contain coloured pigments that give colour to plant parts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking chromoplasts with coloured pigments or colour.

rubric.why: Names a plastid type and its function.
rubric.description: Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store food.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking leucoplasts with food storage.

modelAnswer: Plastids are membrane-bound organelles found in plant cells and are enclosed by a double membrane.
A chloroplast contains a fluid matrix called the stroma.
Its internal membrane sacs, called thylakoids, are arranged in stacks called grana and contain chlorophyll.
Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis; chromoplasts contain coloured pigments that give colour to plant parts.
Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store food such as starch, oils or proteins.

items.followUp: What is an organ? Give one example of an organ and identify its tissues.

rubric.why: Defines tissue in terms of its cells and their work.
rubric.description: A tissue is a group of similar cells that perform the same function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining a tissue as similar cells working together for a common function.

rubric.why: Illustrates the tissue level with an example and its function.
rubric.description: For example, muscle tissue consists of cells that contract and bring about movement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct tissue example and its function.

modelAnswer: At the tissue level, similar cells work together to perform the same function.
For example, muscle tissue is made of cells that contract and bring about movement.
